results.message: What did an ordinary believer feel at the font when they were baptized?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We cannot tell you what an ordinary believer felt standing at the font, save in one real case, and it is not really ordinary. Augustine wrote down his own baptism at Milan, years after it happened, already a bishop, about a conversion he examined at book length. He wept in the hymns and songs. That one first-person account survives. Beyond it, almost nothing does. Both of our own voices are bishops. What reaches us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided about someone, not what an unremarkable person standing in front of him was feeling.

We can tell you what you were taught beforehand. Augustine tells those to be baptized they got the Creed first, to know what to believe, then the Lord's Prayer, to know whom to ask: “He said, ‘How will they call on Him in whom they have not believed?’ That is why you did not receive the Lord’s Prayer first and the Creed after it. You received the Creed first, so that in it you would know what to believe. Then you received the Prayer, so that in it you would know whom to call on. So the Creed belongs to faith, and the Lord’s Prayer to prayer. For it is the one who believes who is heard when he calls.”

You said the Creed back, and then we baptized you. Cyprian taught that baptism washes sin away once, and after that almsgiving became the ordinary remedy for the sin you go on committing.

What was decided we can show you. What an ordinary person felt from inside, we cannot.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258
